claim: Mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are intrinsically incapable of producing type I interferons (IFNs).
source: When mammalian cells detect a viral infection, they initiate a type I interferon (IFNs) response as part of their innate immune system. This antiviral mechanism is conserved in virtually all cell types, except for embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and oocytes which are intrinsically incapable of producing IFNs.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as established background; supported by citations in introduction

claim: In the absence of miRNAs, ESCs acquire an active IFN response.
source: Here we show that, in the absence of miRNAs, ESCs acquire an active IFN response.
evidence: Main finding stated in abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3

claim: MAVS is actively silenced by miRNAs in ESCs.
source: Proteomic analysis identified MAVS, a central component of the IFN pathway, to be actively silenced by miRNAs and responsible for suppressing IFN expression in ESCs.
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis and Western blot data shown in Figure 3

claim: Knocking out miR-673 restores the antiviral response in ESCs through MAVS regulation.
source: Furthermore, we show that knocking out a single miRNA, miR-673, restores the antiviral response in ESCs through MAVS regulation.
evidence: Supported by CRISPR knockout experiments and viral susceptibility assays shown in Figure 5

claim: The interaction between miR-673 and MAVS acts as a switch to suppress the antiviral IFN during pluripotency.
source: Our findings suggest that the interaction between miR-673 and MAVS acts as a switch to suppress the antiviral IFN during pluripotency and present genetic approaches to enhance their antiviral immunity.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data showing miR-673 regulation of MAVS and its effects on IFN response

claim: Type I IFNs activate the JAK-STAT pathway and production of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) in infected and neighboring cells.
source: Once type I IFNs are secreted, they activate the JAK-STAT pathway and production of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) in both the infected and neighbouring cells to induce an antiviral state (Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2015).

claim: RIG-I and MDA5 initiate a signaling cascade through MAVS that activates Ifnb1 transcription.
source: The dsRNA sensors RIG-I and MDA5 initiate a signalling cascade that signals through the central mitochondrial-associated factor MAVS, ultimately activating Ifnb1 transcription.

claim: The cGAS/STING pathway is activated upon detection of viral or foreign DNA molecules.
source: The cGAS/STING pathway is activated upon detection of viral or other foreign DNA molecules and uses a distinct signalling pathway involving the endoplasmic reticulum associated STING protein (Chan and Gack, 2016).
evidence: Established pathway mechanism cited from literature

claim: Both mouse and human embryonic stem cells fail to produce IFNs.
source: Both mouse and human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Wang et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2010) as well as embryonic carcinoma cells (Burke et al., 1978) fail to produce IFNs, suggesting that this function is acquired during differentiation.

claim: ESCs are protected from viral infections by the trophoblast in their natural setting.
source: The rationale for silencing this response is not fully understood but it has been proposed that in their natural setting, ESCs are protected from viral infections by the trophoblast, which forms the outer layer of the blastocyst (Delorme-Axford et al., 2014).

claim: ESCs exhibit a mild response to exogenous IFNs.
source: ESCs exhibit a mild response to exogenous IFNs, suggesting that during embryonic development, maternal IFN could have protective properties (Hong and Carmichael, 2013; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: A Dicer-dependent RNA interference mechanism functions as an alternative antiviral mechanism in mouse ESCs.
source: In mouse ESCs, a Dicer-dependent RNA interference (RNAi) mechanism, reminiscent to that of plants and insects, is suggested to function as an alternative antiviral mechanism (Maillard et al., 2013).

claim: Human ESCs intrinsically express high levels of a subgroup of ISGs in the absence of infection.
source: And in humans, ESCs intrinsically express high levels of a subgroup of ISGs in the absence of infection, bypassing the need for an antiviral IFN response (Wu et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2012).

claim: Silencing of the IFN response during pluripotency may prevent aberrant IFN production in response to retrotransposons and endogenous retroviral derived dsRNA.
source: Silencing of the IFN response during pluripotency may also be essential to avoid aberrant IFN production in response to retrotransposons and endogenous retroviral derived dsRNA, which are highly expressed during the early stages of embryonic development and oocytes (Ahmad et al., 2018; Grow et al., 2015; Macia et al., 2015; Peaston et al., 2004; Macfarlan et al., 2012).

claim: Exposing cells to exogenous IFN induces differentiation and an anti-proliferative state.
source: Furthermore, exposing cells to exogenous IFN induces differentiation and an anti-proliferative state, which would have catastrophic consequences during very early embryonic development (Borden et al., 1982; Hertzog et al., 1994).

claim: miRNAs are essential for successful differentiation of ESCs.
source: One particular class of regulatory factors that are essential for the successful differentiation of ESCs are miRNAs (Greve et al., 2013).

claim: miRNAs originate from long precursor RNA molecules that undergo two consecutive processing steps.
source: These type of small RNAs originate from long precursor RNA molecules, which undergo two consecutive processing steps, one in the nucleus by the Microprocessor complex, followed by a DICER-mediated processing in the cytoplasm (Treiber et al., 2018).

claim: The Microprocessor complex is composed of DGCR8 and DROSHA, both essential for mature miRNA production.
source: The Microprocessor complex is composed of the dsRNA binding protein DGCR8 and the RNase III DROSHA which are both essential for mature miRNA production (Gregory et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2003).

claim: Mammalian DICER is essential for production of siRNAs.
source: In addition, mammalian DICER is also essential for production of siRNAs (Bernstein et al., 2001).

claim: Genetic ablation of Dgcr8 or Dicer in mice blocks ESC differentiation.
source: The genetic ablation of Dgcr8 or Dicer in mice blocks ESCs differentiation suggesting that miRNAs are an essential factor for this, as these are the common substrates for the two RNA processing factors (Wang et al., 2007; Kanellopoulou et al., 2005).

claim: miRNAs are responsible for suppressing the IFN response during pluripotency, specifically to immunostimulatory RNAs.
source: In this study, we show that miRNAs are responsible for suppressing the IFN response during pluripotency, specifically to immunostimulatory RNAs.
evidence: Main finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3

claim: miRNA-deficient ESCs are able to synthesize IFN-β and mount a functional antiviral response.
source: We found that miRNA-deficient ESCs acquire an IFN-proficient state, are able to synthesize IFN-β and mount a functional antiviral response.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2

claim: miRNAs specifically downregulate MAVS in ESCs.
source: Our results show that miRNAs specifically downregulate MAVS (mitochondrial antiviral signalling protein), an essential and central protein in the IFN response pathway.
evidence: Supported by proteomic and Western blot data in Figure 3

claim: ESCs with increased MAVS expression show increased IFN production and antiviral response.
source: In agreement, ESCs with increased MAVS expression or knock-out of the MAVS-regulating miRNA miR-673, resulted in an increased IFN production and antiviral response.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5

claim: Mouse ESCs do not produce type I IFNs in response to poly(I:C) transfection.
source: It has been shown that mouse ESCs do not produce type I IFNs in response to poly(I:C) transfection, a synthetic analogue of dsRNA classically used to mimic viral RNA replication intermediates (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from literature and confirmed by experimental data in Figure 1A

claim: Transfection of poly(I:C) did not result in Ifnb1 expression in both ESC lines (ESC1 and ESC2).
source: As expected, the transfection of poly(I:C) did not result in Ifnb1 expression in both ESC lines (Figure 1A).

claim: ESCs failed to activate Ifnb1 expression upon G3-YSD transfection.
source: ESCs also failed to activate Ifnb1 expression upon G3-YSD transfection, suggesting that the cGAS/STING pathway was also inactive (Figure 1B).

claim: NIH3T3 cells did not express Ifnb1 in response to G3-YSD.
source: Similarly, NIH3T3 cells, which have also been previously shown to have a defect in this specific pathway (Cheng et al., 2018), did not express Ifnb1 in response to G3-YSD (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1B, supported by citation

claim: ESCs are at least 30 times more sensitive to TMEV infection than NIH3T3 and BV-2 cells.
source: These same cell lines were infected with the (+) ssRNA virus TMEV (Theiler's Murine Encephalomyelitis Virus) and showed that ESCs are at least 30 times more sensitive than NIH3T3 and BV-2 cells, which correlates with the ability of these cell lines to induce Ifnb1mRNA expression (Figure 1C).

claim: The ability of cells to express IFN in response to viruses or immunogenic nucleic acids is acquired during differentiation.
source: The ability of cells to express IFN in response to viruses or immunogenic nucleic acids is assumed to be acquired during differentiation.

claim: Pluripotency markers Nanog and Pou5f1 showed a rapid decrease in mRNA expression during differentiation in both ESC lines.
source: The pluripotency markers Nanog and Pou5f1 (Oct4) showed a rapid decrease in mRNA expression during differentiation in both the cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), whereas differentiation markers Neurog2, Gata6 and Gata4 showed a gradual increase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) confirming successful differentiation of the ESCs.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Differentiation markers Neurog2, Gata6 and Gata4 showed a gradual increase during ESC differentiation.
source: The pluripotency markers Nanog and Pou5f1 (Oct4) showed a rapid decrease in mRNA expression during differentiation in both the cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), whereas differentiation markers Neurog2, Gata6 and Gata4 showed a gradual increase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) confirming successful differentiation of the ESCs.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Differentiated ESCs acquired the ability to synthesize Ifnb1 to similar levels as BV-2 cells.
source: Next, we compared the ability of ESCs (day 0) and retinoic-acid differentiated cells after 10 days (day 10) to express Ifnb1 mRNA in response to poly(I:C), and confirmed that differentiated cells acquired the ability to synthesize Ifnb1 to similar levels to the positive control cell line, BV-2 (Figure 1D).

claim: Dicer-/- ESCs were more resistant to viruses compared to their wild-type counterparts.
source: Unexpectedly, Dicer-/- ESCs were more resistant to viruses compared to their wild-type counterparts (previously named ESC2) (Figure 2A, left).

claim: Similar results of increased viral resistance were obtained using Influenza A virus in Dicer-/- ESCs.
source: Similar results were obtained using the (-) ssRNA virus, Influenza A (IAV) (Figure 2A, right).

claim: The absence of Dgcr8 decreased TMEV and IAV viral susceptibility.
source: The absence of Dgcr8 also decreased TMEV and IAV viral susceptibility, suggesting that miRNAs are responsible for suppressing the antiviral response in ESCs (Figure 2A).

claim: Dgcr8-/- cells were more resistant to virus infection than Dicer-/- cells.
source: Interestingly, Dgcr8-/- cells were more resistant to virus infection than Dicer-/- cells, which supports a dual function for DICER by also acting as a direct antiviral factor targeting viral transcripts for degradation by RNAi.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2A with interpretation

claim: ESCs lacking miRNAs (Dgcr8-/- or Dicer-/-) were able to respond to poly(I:C) and express Ifnb1 mRNA and protein in a dose dependent manner.
source: ESCs lacking miRNAs (Dgcr8-/- or Dicer-/-) were able to respond to the dsRNA analogue, poly(I:C) and express Ifnb1 mRNA and protein in a dose dependent manner (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C), whereas no significant response was observed with immunostimulatory DNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental results shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: No significant response to immunostimulatory DNA was observed in miRNA-deficient ESCs.
source: ESCs lacking miRNAs (Dgcr8-/- or Dicer-/-) were able to respond to the dsRNA analogue, poly(I:C) and express Ifnb1 mRNA and protein in a dose dependent manner (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C), whereas no significant response was observed with immunostimulatory DNA (Figure 2B).

claim: Blocking IFN signaling using Ruxolitinib significantly increased viral replication in miRNA-deficient ESCs but not in wild-type ESCs.
source: To further establish the involvement of IFN expression in these observations, we blocked IFN signalling using the JAK1/2 inhibitor Ruxolitinib before infecting cells with TMEV. As a result we observed no, or a very mild increase in TMEV viral replication in wild-type ESCs, but a significant increase in viral replication in miRNA-deficient ESCs (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D

claim: Mouse ESCs retain the ability to respond to external IFNs.
source: ESCs were also stimulated with exogenous IFN-β and confirmed that mouse ESCs retain the ability to respond to external IFNs, and, importantly, that miRNA deficiency did not alter ISG expression levels, supporting the hypothesis that the miRNA-mediated silencing of the IFN pathway in ESCs occurs upstream of IFN production (Figure 2D).

claim: miRNA deficiency did not alter ISG expression levels in response to exogenous IFN-β.
source: ESCs were also stimulated with exogenous IFN-β and confirmed that mouse ESCs retain the ability to respond to external IFNs, and, importantly, that miRNA deficiency did not alter ISG expression levels, supporting the hypothesis that the miRNA-mediated silencing of the IFN pathway in ESCs occurs upstream of IFN production (Figure 2D).

claim: Rescue of Dgcr8 and Dicer knock-out cell lines reverted to wild-type viral replication and susceptibility levels.
source: To verify that the observed results are solely due to the absence of miRNAs, we rescued the knock-out cell lines by reintroducing Dgcr8 and Dicer and observed that these reverted to wild-type viral replication and susceptibility levels (Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E

claim: The inhibitors BX795 and BMS345541 increased viral susceptibility far more in knock-out cell lines than in wild-type cell lines.
source: Both inhibitors increased viral susceptibility in wild-type cells lines, however, the effect was far greater in the knock-out cell lines (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that miRNAs regulate the interferon pathway upstream Ifnb1 transcription.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: miRNAs regulate the interferon pathway upstream of Ifnb1 transcription.
source: Both inhibitors increased viral susceptibility in wild-type cells lines, however, the effect was far greater in the knock-out cell lines (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that miRNAs regulate the interferon pathway upstream Ifnb1 transcription.
evidence: Inference from experimental results shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: Proteomic analysis revealed significant differences in ribosome structure/function, mitochondrial activity and oxidative phosphorylation pathways between Dgcr8-/- and rescued cell lines.
source: STRING analyses of the expression profiles revealed significant differences in a number of pathways, including ribosome structure/function, mitochondrial activity and the oxidative phosphorylation pathway, which were downregulated in the absence of miRNAs (Figure 3C, for complete list see Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Proteomic analysis result shown in Figure 3C

claim: MAVS was upregulated in the absence of miRNAs.
source: A search for differentially expressed proteins involved in the IFN response did not reveal any significant changes except for the Mitochondrial antiviral-signalling protein (MAVS), which in contrast to many other mitochondria-related proteins, was upregulated in the absence of miRNAs.

claim: MAVS was the only factor consistently expressed to higher levels in both miRNA-deficient cell lines, Dgcr8-/- and Dicer-/-.
source: Western blot and qRT-PCR analysis confirmed that MAVS was the only factor consistently expressed to higher levels in both miRNA-deficient cell lines, Dgcr8-/- and Dicer-/- (Figure 3D, lanes 2 and 5, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), compared to a panel of other components of the same innate immune response pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Western blot and qRT-PCR results shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F

claim: Only the Mavs 3'UTR showed relatively higher luciferase expression levels in the knock-out lines compared to the empty plasmid.
source: Only the Mavs 3'UTR showed relatively higher luciferase expression levels in the knock-out lines when compared to the empty plasmid, suggesting that the 3'UTR of Mavs is strongly regulated by miRNAs in ESCs (Figure 4A).
evidence: Luciferase assay result shown in Figure 4A

claim: Overexpression of miRNA-resistant MAVS in wild-type ESCs resulted in a 15-fold decrease in TCID50 and significant reduction in vRNA levels compared to wild-type ESCs.
source: For this reason, a miRNA-resistant form of Mavs, lacking its natural 3'UTR, was overexpressed in wild-type ESCs and infected with TMEV to test if cells regain viral resistance similar to miRNA deficient ESCs (Figure 4B). A 15-fold decrease in TCID50 and significant reduction in vRNA levels were found compared to wild-type ESCs (Figure 4C).

claim: MAVS overexpressing cells regained the ability to produce Ifnb1 after stimulation with poly(I:C).
source: MAVS overexpressing cells also regained the ability to produce Ifnb1 after stimulation with poly(I:C) (Figure 4D).

claim: MAVS is a crucial target for the absence of the IFN response in ESCs.
source: All these experiments show that MAVS is a crucial target for the absence of the IFN response in ESCs.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental results in Figure 4

claim: Transfection of miR-125a-5p, miR-125b-5p, miR-185-5p and miR-673-5p mimics in Dgcr8-/- cells resulted in reductions in MAVS protein and mRNA levels.
source: We transfected Dgcr8-/- cells with mimics of these miRNAs and measured Mavs mRNA and protein levels by RT-qPCR and western blot, respectively. Results showed reductions in MAVS protein and mRNA levels for all tested miRNAs (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Infection of miRNA-transfected Dgcr8-/- cells with TMEV resulted in an increase in both susceptibility and viral replication for miR-125a-5p, miR-125b-5p and miR-673-5p.
source: The infection of miRNA-transfected Dgcr8-/- cells with TMEV resulted in an increase in both susceptibility and viral replication for miR-125a-5p, miR-125b-5p and miR-673–5p, which correlated with the ability of these miRNAs to downregulate MAVS protein levels (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Transfection of Dgcr8+/+ cells with anti-miR-673-5p showed a clear increase in MAVS protein expression.
source: As an alternative approach, Dgcr8+/+ cells were transfected with inhibitors to miRNAs miR-125a-5p, miR-125b-5p and miR-673–5p. Western blot analysis showed a clear increase in MAVS protein expression, especially for anti-miR-673–5p (Figure 5C).

claim: miR-673 is a crucial miRNA involved in MAVS regulation.
source: Because miR-673–5p showed the largest effect on MAVS protein expression both when depleted and overexpressed, we hypothesize that miR-673 is a crucial miRNA involved on MAVS regulation.
evidence: Inference from experimental results in Figure 5A,C

claim: The absence of miR-673-5p was enough to observe an increase in MAVS expression both at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: The absence of miR-673–5p was enough to observe an increase in MAVS expression both at the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: Mouse fibroblasts (NIH3T3) had no detectable miR-673-5p.
source: In addition, we measured miR-673 and MAVS expression levels in the mouse fibroblasts cell line, NIH3T3, which is proficient in producing IFN in response to dsRNA. Mouse fibroblasts had no detectable miR-673–5p, and MAVS protein expression was comparable to miRNA-deficient ESC (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), highlighting the correlation of MAVS expression with the ability of cells to activate Ifnb1 expression in response to immunogenic RNA.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: MAVS protein expression in NIH3T3 cells was comparable to miRNA-deficient ESCs.
source: In addition, we measured miR-673 and MAVS expression levels in the mouse fibroblasts cell line, NIH3T3, which is proficient in producing IFN in response to dsRNA. Mouse fibroblasts had no detectable miR-673–5p, and MAVS protein expression was comparable to miRNA-deficient ESC (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), highlighting the correlation of MAVS expression with the ability of cells to activate Ifnb1 expression in response to immunogenic RNA.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: miR-673-deficient cell lines showed a consistent decrease in virus replication, similar to that observed in the absence of all miRNAs (Dgcr8-/-).
source: Next, miR-673-deficient cell lines were tested for TMEV susceptibility, which showed a consistent decrease in virus replication, similar to that observed in the absence of all miRNAs (Dgcr8-/-), suggesting this miRNA is essential in regulating the innate antiviral response in ESCs (Figure 5E).

claim: miR-673 is essential in regulating the innate antiviral response in ESCs.
source: Next, miR-673-deficient cell lines were tested for TMEV susceptibility, which showed a consistent decrease in virus replication, similar to that observed in the absence of all miRNAs (Dgcr8-/-), suggesting this miRNA is essential in regulating the innate antiviral response in ESCs (Figure 5E).
evidence: Inference from experimental result shown in Figure 5E

claim: Inhibition of IFN signaling did not significantly increase the accumulation of viral RNA in wild-type ESCs (Dgcr8+/+).
source: Whereas inhibition of IFN signalling did not significantly increase the accumulation of viral RNA in wild-type ESCs (Dgcr8+/+), both miR-673-deficient and Dgcr8-/- ESCs showed a significant increase in viral RNA upon treatment, confirming the role of miR-673 and IFNs in viral susceptibility (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A

claim: Both miR-673-deficient and Dgcr8-/- ESCs showed a significant increase in viral RNA upon Ruxolitinib treatment.
source: Whereas inhibition of IFN signalling did not significantly increase the accumulation of viral RNA in wild-type ESCs (Dgcr8+/+), both miR-673-deficient and Dgcr8-/- ESCs showed a significant increase in viral RNA upon treatment, confirming the role of miR-673 and IFNs in viral susceptibility (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A

claim: Knocking out miR-673-5p expression did not affect the ability of ESCs to proliferate or induce spontaneous differentiation.
source: As controls, we confirmed that knocking out miR-673–5p expression did not affect the ability of ESCs to proliferate or induced spontaneous differentiation, which could cause differences in viral susceptibility (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–E).
evidence: Control experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–E

claim: During ESC differentiation with retinoic acid, expression of miR-673-5p became silenced.
source: Interestingly, during ESC differentiation with retinoic acid, expression of miR-673–5p became silenced, confirming previous results obtained with alternative differentiation protocols (Knelangen et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2014; Hadjimichael et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016), and suggesting that the expression levels of this miRNA negatively correlate with the ability of cells to activate the IFN response (Figure 5G).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5G, supported by citations

claim: The expression levels of miR-673 negatively correlate with the ability of cells to activate the IFN response.
source: Interestingly, during ESC differentiation with retinoic acid, expression of miR-673–5p became silenced, confirming previous results obtained with alternative differentiation protocols (Knelangen et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2014; Hadjimichael et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016), and suggesting that the expression levels of this miRNA negatively correlate with the ability of cells to activate the IFN response (Figure 5G).
evidence: Inference from experimental result shown in Figure 5G

claim: The IFN response in mouse ESCs is silenced by the post-transcriptional control of Mavs expression by miR-673-5p.
source: Collectively, these data show that the IFN response in mouse ESCs is silenced by the post-transcriptional control of Mavs expression by miR-673–5p.

claim: The pluripotent state of a cell is incompatible with an active IFN response.
source: Several studies suggest that the pluripotent state of a cell is incompatible with an active IFN response (Guo et al., 2015).

claim: Reprogramming of somatic cells to iPSCs leads to a loss of IFN response.
source: In agreement, reprogramming of somatic cells to iPSCs (induced pluripotent stem cells) leads to a loss of IFN response, suggesting the presence of regulatory mechanisms able to switch this antiviral pathway on or off between the differentiated and pluripotent states (Chen et al., 2012).

claim: Mammalian pluripotent stem cells, iPSCs and embryonic carcinoma cells exhibit an attenuated production of ISGs upon type I IFN stimulation.
source: Mammalian pluripotent stem cells, iPSCs and embryonic carcinoma cells exhibit an attenuated production of ISGs upon type I IFN stimulation (Hong and Carmichael, 2013; Irudayam et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014; Burke et al., 1978).

claim: Type I IFN stimulation could impair ESC self-renewal capacity.
source: Why these activities are supressed is still not understood, but it has been hypothesized that type I IFN stimulation could impair their self-renewal capacity, since these compounds are well-known antiproliferative agents and inducers of cell death (Bekisz et al., 2010).

claim: Type I IFNs are capable of inhibiting tumour cell division in vitro.
source: Indeed, type I IFNs are capable of inhibiting tumour cell division in vitro and are currently employed as an adjuvant to treat several types of cancers, acting as stimulants of the innate immune cellular response (Bracci et al., 2017).

claim: Mouse ESCs express low levels of the RNA sensors TLR3, MDA5 and RIG-I.
source: Mouse ESCs express low levels of the RNA sensors TLR3, MDA5 and RIG-I, which could explain their inability to respond to dsRNA although no functional studies support this model so far (Wang et al., 2013).

claim: The overexpression of a miRNA-resistant form of MAVS in wild-type ESCs is enough to enable dsRNA-mediated IFN activation.
source: Our data shows an alternative scenario in which MAVS is the key factor for controlling the IFN response. The overexpression of a miRNA-resistant form of MAVS in wild-type ESCs is enough to enable dsRNA-mediated IFN activation, suggesting that dsRNA sensing is not a limiting step in the IFN pathway in ESCs.

claim: dsRNA sensing is not a limiting step in the IFN pathway in ESCs.
source: Our data shows an alternative scenario in which MAVS is the key factor for controlling the IFN response. The overexpression of a miRNA-resistant form of MAVS in wild-type ESCs is enough to enable dsRNA-mediated IFN activation, suggesting that dsRNA sensing is not a limiting step in the IFN pathway in ESCs.
evidence: Inference from experimental result in Figure 4

claim: Regulation of MAVS alone is an efficient mechanism to block dsRNA induced IFN expression compared to suppressing individual dsRNA sensors.
source: Regulation of MAVS alone proves to be an efficient mechanism to block dsRNA induced IFN expression compared to suppressing individual dsRNA sensors.

claim: miRNAs only suppress RNA-mediated IFN activation, but not the DNA-mediated pathway.
source: The observation that miRNAs only suppress RNA-mediated IFN activation, but not the DNA-mediated pathway, leads us to speculate about the reasons for silencing this specific response during pluripotency.

claim: Embryonic stem cells and earlier stages of embryonic development are characterized by high expression levels of specific retrotransposons and endogenous retroviruses.
source: Embryonic stem cells, and also earlier stages of embryonic development are characterized by high expression levels of specific retrotransposons (non-LTR) and endogenous retroviruses (LTR), which are a hallmark of their pluripotent state. This is in contrast to most somatic cell types that silence their expression (Yin et al., 2018).

claim: Silencing the RNA-mediated IFN response during pluripotency would act as a protective mechanism for aberrant IFN activation by transposon-derived transcripts.
source: Therefore, silencing the RNA-mediated IFN response during pluripotency would act as a protective mechanism for aberrant IFN activation by transposon-derived transcripts.
evidence: Hypothesis based on literature and experimental results

claim: The endonuclease DICER can act as an antiviral factor in mouse ESCs by generating antiviral siRNAs.
source: The endonuclease DICER can act as an antiviral factor in mouse ESCs by generating antiviral siRNAs (Maillard et al., 2013).

claim: Detection of antiviral DICER activity is facilitated in the absence of a competent IFN response.
source: Detection of antiviral DICER activity is facilitated in the absence of a competent IFN response, such as in the case of pluripotent cells, but also in somatic cells where the type I IFN response has been genetically impaired (Maillard et al., 2016).

claim: In IFN-competent cells, the RNA sensor LGP2 acts as an inhibitor of DICER cleavage activity on dsRNA.
source: These findings are supported by the observation that in IFN-competent cells, the RNA sensor LGP2 acts as an inhibitor of DICER cleavage activity on dsRNA (van der Veen et al., 2018).

claim: When Dicer is disrupted in ESCs, they become more resistant by acquiring an active IFN response.
source: Interestingly, when we disrupt Dicer in ESCs, which inherently lack an IFN response and would theoretically render these cells highly sensitive to viral infections, they become more resistant by acquiring an active IFN response.

claim: Cells have developed mechanisms to compensate for the loss of a specific antiviral pathway.
source: All these results support the presence of extensive cross-talk between the different antiviral strategies, and suggests that cells have developed mechanisms to compensate for the loss of a specific antiviral pathway.
evidence: Inference from experimental results and literature

claim: MAVS and miR-673 levels are the key factors regulating the IFN response to dsRNAs during pluripotency.
source: Our model shows that MAVS and miR-673 levels are the key factors regulating the IFN response to dsRNAs during pluripotency.

claim: Overexpressing MAVS or knocking-out miR-673 in ESCs is enough to enhance their antiviral response.
source: Accordingly, overexpressing MAVS or knocking-out this single miRNA in ESCs is enough to enhance their antiviral response.

claim: miR-673 is only conserved in rodents.
source: Interestingly, this miRNA is only conserved in rodents, despite human ESCs also suppressing type I IFNs expression (Hong and Carmichael, 2013).
evidence: Stated as fact with citation for human ESC IFN suppression

claim: Either other miRNAs regulate MAVS expression in human ESCs, or alternative mechanisms operate to silence IFN.
source: This suggests that either other miRNAs regulate MAVS expression in human ESCs, or alternative mechanisms operate to silence IFN.

claim: Human and mouse ESCs have been suggested to constitutively express a subset of ISGs to protect them from viruses.
source: Interestingly, human and mouse ESCs have been suggested to constitutively express a subset of ISGs to protect them from viruses (Wu et al., 2018).

claim: miRNAs did not significantly affect production of ISGs such as IFITM1, IFTIM2, IFITM3 in ESCs.
source: Our proteomics data suggest that, from all the ISGs detected, miRNAs did not significantly affect production of these antiviral factors, such as IFITM1, IFTIM2, IFITM3 amongst others.

claim: Engineering ESCs to acquire a functional IFN response significantly increases their antiviral immunity.
source: We have shown that engineering ESCs to acquire a functional IFN response significantly increases their antiviral immunity, highlighting the powerful antiviral effects of IFNs even during pluripotency.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental results in Figures 4 and 5

claim: DICER and miRNAs act as negative regulators of the IFN response in human and mouse models outside pluripotency.
source: Previous findings also support a general role for DICER and miRNAs acting as negative regulators of the IFN response in human and mouse models outside pluripotency (Papadopoulou et al., 2012; Witteveldt et al., 2018).

claim: Overexpressing the viral protein VP55 from Vaccinia virus to deplete cellular miRNAs showed that miRNAs are relevant to control the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines during viral chronic infections, but not in the acute antiviral response.
source: In agreement, an indirect approach to deplete cellular miRNAs, by overexpressing the viral protein VP55 from Vaccinia virus, showed that miRNAs are also relevant to control the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines during viral chronic infections, but not in the acute antiviral response (Aguado et al., 2015).

claim: DICER1-/- HEK293T human cell line has an attenuated IFN response due to low PRRs expression.
source: It is relevant to mention that some of the results leading to this conclusion have been primarily generated in DICER1-/- HEK293T human cell line (Bogerd et al., 2014; Tsai et al., 2018), which has an attenuated IFN response due to low PRRs expression (Rice et al., 2014; Witteveldt et al., 2018).
